newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China ship postpones entry into Taiwan port.
newsitem.headline: China ship postpones entry into Taiwan port.

text.p: A dispute over flag-flying has postponed the arrival of the second Chinese ship sailing directly to Taiwan, port and shipping officials said on Sunday.

Although Saturday's long-awaited first crossing from China to Taiwan went smoothly, problems emerged on Sunday as the second ship to make the voyage grappled with a maritime custom which calls for ships to fly the flag of their host port.
The custom carries political implications on the revived shipping route. Taiwan split from China following a civil war in 1949 and Beijing regards Taiwan as a renegade province.

The China-owned, St. Vincent-registered Far East Glory would become the second Chinese ship to make an authorised crossing of the ideological divide to Taiwan in 48 years, following the Sheng Da on Saturday.

"According to its notice, the ship was supposed to enter Kaohsiung Habour at 11:00 a.m. (0300 GMT), but its Taiwan agent later applied to postpone the entry time to 4:00 p.m. (0800 GMT)," a Kaohsiung Harbour duty officer told Reuters.
The official declined to comment on whether it was to avoid the sensitive flag issue.
But shippers said the delay would allow the Far East Glory to enter after dark when flags are traditionally lowered, thereby avoiding the flag issue.

On Saturday, the Sheng Da removed Taiwan's Nationalist Republic of China flag after briefly flying it as it entered Kaohsiung port. Taiwan harbour officials said the flag was removed because the Sheng Da entered Taiwan at night.
"There is no point flying the flag at night," Yu Fang-lai, director of Kaohsiung Harbour Bureau, told reporters.
Shipping company officials said both the China-owned Sheng Da and Far East Glory were reluctant to fly the Taiwanese flag because of the sensitive political meaning behind it.

"The two rival sides have sharply divided ideologically and politically, and it was natural that the mainland ships were reluctant to fly the (Nationalist) Republic of China flag," a shipping company supervisor told Reuters by telephone.
"Flying the flag is tantamount to recognising the sovereignty of Taiwan," the offical said on condition of anonymity.
He said Taiwan tolerated the Sheng Da's act because it hoped the direct sailing could be a first step to improve relations between the two rivals.
